exercises.title: Gentle breathing
exercises.summary: Slow your breathing to a comfortable, steady rhythm.

steps.text: Settle into a comfortable position. Let your shoulders drop.
Breathe in through your nose for a count of four.
Breathe out slowly for a count of six. Let the out-breath be longer.
Keep this rhythm. If your mind wanders, return to counting.
Let your breathing return to its own pace. Notice how you feel.

exercises.techniqueSource: Paced breathing with a longer exhale (NCCIH relaxation techniques)

exercises.title: Body scan
exercises.summary: Move your attention slowly from your feet to your head.

steps.text: Lie down and let the bed take your weight.
Notice your feet and ankles. Let them soften.
Move your attention to your legs and hips.
Notice your belly and chest rising and falling.
Soften your hands, arms and shoulders.
Relax your jaw, your eyes and your forehead.
Rest here, aware of your whole body.

exercises.techniqueSource: Body scan (VA Whole Health mindfulness practice)

exercises.title: Five quiet minutes
exercises.summary: For when you wake in the night. No need to fall asleep; just rest.

steps.text: You're awake, and that's okay. There's nothing you need to do.
Breathe out slowly, a little longer than you breathe in.
Notice three things you can feel: the pillow, the blanket, your breath.
If thoughts come, let them pass like clouds.
Rest your eyes. Resting is enough.

exercises.techniqueSource: Grounding and paced breathing (NCCIH relaxation techniques)

exercises.title: Morning reflection
exercises.summary: A short check-in with yourself to start the day gently.

steps.text: Before you reach for your phone's other apps, take three slow breaths.
Notice how your body feels right now, without judging it.
Pick one small thing you'd like to do for yourself today.
Open a curtain or step outside for a minute of daylight if you can.

exercises.techniqueSource: Morning light and brief reflection (CDC sleep guidance)

articles.title: Why a steady bedtime helps
articles.summary: Going to bed and getting up at similar times can make sleep feel easier.
articles.body:
Your body keeps an internal clock. When bedtimes and wake times move around a lot, that clock has to keep adjusting.

Try keeping your wake time within about an hour each day, including weekends. A steady morning tends to make evenings steadier too.

If a night goes badly, you don't need to make it up by sleeping in. Get up at your usual time and be gentle with yourself.

articles.title: What your watch is estimating
articles.summary: Sleep stages from a wearable are estimates, not measurements.
articles.body:
Watches and rings estimate sleep stages from movement and heart rate. They are useful for spotting patterns over many nights, but a single night's numbers can be off.

How you feel in the morning matters as much as any chart. Stillmoon always shows your own check-in next to what a device estimated.

articles.title: When to talk to a doctor
articles.summary: Some sleep difficulties are worth mentioning to a healthcare professional.
articles.body:
If you've had trouble falling or staying asleep most nights for several weeks, it can help to talk with a doctor or another qualified healthcare professional.

It's also worth mentioning loud, frequent snoring, or feeling very sleepy during the day even after a full night in bed.

Stillmoon can't diagnose sleep conditions. A professional can look at the whole picture with you.
